lead: Today the Great Fast opens into the Week of the Passion, and the Church walks with her King into Jerusalem. The four readings follow one question: what kind of king? Jacob promises that the scepter will stay with Judah, and pictures a donkey’s colt tied to a vine. Zechariah sees the king come, humble, on that very animal, and bringing peace in place of chariots. Paul reminds the Gentile believers that they live from Israel’s root, grafted in by grace, and must not boast. Matthew shows Jesus riding into the city to the cry of Hosanna, going straight to the Temple, and healing the blind and the lame. The key words are scepter, humble, root and Hosanna.

set: Jacob is about to die in Egypt. He gathers his twelve sons and tells them “what will happen to you in days to come” (49:1). This is the Testament of Jacob, a poem that many scholars consider very old, in which each son stands for a future tribe. Some of the words are hard to understand, and translations differ. The reading takes the two longest blessings: Judah, who will rule, and Joseph, who suffered and was upheld.
str: v. 8: Judah praised by his brothers.
v. 9: the lion.
v. 10: the scepter.
vv. 11–12: a picture of plenty: vines, wine and milk.
vv. 22–24: Joseph, fruitful and attacked, made strong by the Mighty One of Jacob.
vv. 25–26: the blessings on the head of Joseph.
kw: A play on the name Judah (yᵉhûdâ), which Genesis has linked with praise (29:35). The tribe’s very name is a promise.

The ruler’s staff, a sign of royal authority. David came from Judah, and Israel looked to a future king from his line. The Letter to the Hebrews notes that “our Lord was descended from Judah” (Hebrews 7:14).
An ancient title of God (v. 24), found again in Isaiah 49:26 and Psalm 132:2. Joseph’s strength was never his own.
vv: Judah is a lion’s whelp;

The Book of Revelation takes up this picture: “the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered”. When John turns to look, he sees a Lamb, standing as if slaughtered (Revelation 5:5–6). That is the surprise of today’s Gospel as well.
The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor the ruler’s staff from between his feet, until tribute comes to him;

A note on the text: the Hebrew here is famously difficult (literally “until Shiloh comes”). The NRSV reads it, by a small change, as “until tribute comes to him”. The ancient Greek and Syriac versions read “until he comes to whom it belongs”, and the POC is close to that: “until its heir comes”. Ancient Jewish tradition, in the Targums, also read the verse of the King Messiah. So do the Fathers.
Binding his foal to the vine and his donkey’s colt to the choice vine,

Only a very rich man could tie an animal to a vine and let it eat. It is a picture of overflowing plenty in the days of this king. Christian readers could not miss the colt today, nor the robe washed “in the blood of grapes”.
Yet his bow remained taut, and his arms were made agile by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob,

The archers suggest the hatred of Joseph’s brothers and all that followed. God stood behind his arms. Joseph was the one “set apart from his brothers” (v. 26), and the one who was rejected became the saviour of his family.
ch: St Justin Martyr, writing to the Roman emperor, reads this prophecy of Jesus: the colt, and the robe washed in the blood of the grape, which points to the blood by which he cleanses those who believe (First Apology 32; in substance). St Augustine sees in the lion who lies down the Christ who laid down his life by his own power, and took it up again (City of God XVI, 41; in substance). Of Joseph, the Catechism recalls his words to his brothers, “it was not you who sent me here, but God”, as an example of God’s providence working through evil (CCC 312). St Ambrose reads him as a figure of Christ (On Joseph; in substance).

r.h: Your king comes to you, humble
set: Chapters 9–14 of Zechariah differ in style from chapters 1–8, and many scholars think they come from a later hand in the years after the return from exile. Israel has no king. Foreign armies pass through the land, and the chapter even names Greece (9:13). Into that situation comes this oracle. It has just described God coming to defend his house (9:8). Now the daughter of Zion is told to shout, because her king is on his way.
str: v. 9: the call to rejoice, and the king.
v. 10: the end of war, and peace to the nations.
v. 11: the blood of the covenant and the prisoners released.
v. 12: “prisoners of hope”, and the promise of double.
kw: The word also means poor, afflicted. This king is on the side of the lowly because he is one of them.
Literally “just and saved” or “just and having victory”. His victory is something God gives him. Matthew’s quotation leaves these two words out and goes straight to “humble”.
the blood of my covenant with you
It recalls Sinai, where Moses sprinkled “the blood of the covenant” (Exodus 24:8). At the supper Jesus will speak of “my blood of the covenant” (Matthew 26:28).
vv: Lo, your king comes to you; triumphant and victorious is he, humble and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey.

A donkey was no shameful animal for a ruler in old Israel; Solomon rode David’s mule to his anointing (1 Kings 1:33). But it is not a warhorse, as the next verse makes clear. In Hebrew verse the second line repeats the first: “on a donkey, on a colt” means one animal.
and the battle bow shall be cut off, and he shall command peace to the nations;
This king disarms his own people, Ephraim in the north and Jerusalem in the south. His rule reaches “from sea to sea”, as in Psalm 72:8, and he wins it by no war.
Return to your stronghold, O prisoners of hope;

A lovely phrase. They are bound, and what binds them is hope. “The waterless pit” (v. 11) recalls the pit into which Joseph was thrown: “the pit was empty; there was no water in it” (Genesis 37:24). In v. 11 the POC calls the prisoners “exiles”.
ch: The Catechism says that the King of glory enters his city riding on a donkey, and that he does not conquer the daughter of Zion, a figure of his Church, by ruse or violence, but by the humility that bears witness to the truth (CCC 559). St Matthew and St John both quote this oracle at the entry (Matthew 21:5; John 12:15). The Church hears in v. 11 the blood of the new covenant, which she receives in the Holy Qurbana (CCC 610–611).

set: Romans 9–11 is Paul’s long wrestling with a question that hurt him deeply: why have most of his own people not accepted Jesus as Messiah? He begins with “great sorrow” (9:2). He has already asked, “has God rejected his people? By no means!” (11:1). He ends by saying that “all Israel will be saved” (11:26), “for the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (11:29). Today’s passage lies between. It is addressed to Gentile Christians in Rome, who may have been tempted to look down on Jews.
str: vv. 13–15: Paul’s mission to the Gentiles is also for the sake of his own people.
v. 16: dough and root.
vv. 17–18: the wild shoot grafted in: do not boast.
vv. 19–22: “stand in awe”: kindness and severity.
vv. 23–24: God can graft them back.
kw: Paul’s hope (v. 14) comes from Deuteronomy 32:21. He wants his people to see in the Gentile Churches what God has promised, and to desire it.
Israel is the cultivated tree of God (compare Jeremiah 11:16). The Gentile is the wild shoot. Paul himself says the grafting is “contrary to nature” (v. 24). It is all grace.
Paul sets both together in v. 22. Apotomia is a cutting off, a word that suits the pruning image. Neither can be used as a claim against anyone else; both are a call to stay in God’s kindness.
vv: If the part of the dough offered as first fruits is holy, then the whole batch is holy; and if the root is holy, then the branches also are holy.
The first image comes from Numbers 15:17–21. The root is most probably the patriarchs, “for the sake of their ancestors” (11:28). The holiness of the root has not been cancelled.
remember that it is not you that support the root, but the root that supports you.
This is the sentence of the passage for Christians. All we have from Abraham, Moses and the prophets, and from Jesus, a son of Israel, we have received through this root.
They were broken off because of their unbelief, but you stand only through faith. So do not become proud, but stand in awe.

Paul is writing to warn the Gentile believer, and he says “some of the branches” (v. 17). He himself is one of the natural branches (11:1). This verse has been misused against the Jewish people, and that misuse is a sin against the text and against them. The tree stands, and they are still its own.
Note then the kindness and the severity of God:
The warning is addressed to the Christian: “otherwise you also will be cut off”. Baptism is a gift to be lived in. Perseverance is itself a grace, for which we ask and in which we must walk.
for God has the power to graft them in again.
The passage ends in hope: “how much more” (v. 24) these natural branches will be grafted into “their own olive tree”.
ch: The Second Vatican Council quotes this image directly: the Church draws sustenance from the root of that well-cultivated olive tree onto which the wild shoots of the Gentiles have been grafted, and the Jews remain most dear to God (Nostra Aetate 4). The Catechism says the same (CCC 60, 755, 839). St John Paul II, visiting the synagogue of Rome in 1986, called the Jewish people our dearly beloved and, in a certain way, elder brothers. So Israel is not replaced. As the Church enters the Week of the Passion, she reads this page to learn humility before the root from which her Lord came.

r.h: Hosanna to the Son of David
set: Jesus has come up from Jericho with the pilgrims going to Jerusalem for Passover (20:17, 29). All four Gospels tell of the entry. The Mount of Olives, east of the city, was linked with the coming of the Lord (Zechariah 14:4). Matthew stresses that this is planned and fulfils Scripture. Unlike the earlier times when Jesus told people to keep silent about who he was (16:20), he now accepts a public acclamation.

Passover brought great crowds to Jerusalem, with memories of liberation and hopes of a king. In the Temple’s outer court, pilgrims bought animals for sacrifice and changed money into the coin accepted for the Temple tax. Doves were the offering of the poor (Leviticus 5:7), the one that Joseph and Mary brought for the child Jesus (Luke 2:24).
str: vv. 1–3: the disciples are sent for the animals.
vv. 4–5: the fulfilment of Scripture.
vv. 6–9: cloaks, branches and the Hosanna.
vv. 10–11: “Who is this?”
vv. 12–13: Jesus clears the Temple.
vv. 14–16: healing, the children, and the anger of the authorities.
v. 17: to Bethany for the night.
kw: Hebrew for “Save, we pray” (Psalm 118:25). By Jesus’ time it was also a cry of joyful greeting. Our Malayalam “Oshana” comes through the Syriac form of the word. The psalm was sung at the great feasts, and it gives the next line as well, “Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord”.
Jesus uses this word of himself: “I am gentle and humble in heart” (11:29), and of the blessed: “the meek” (5:5). It is the key to the entry.
“The whole city was in turmoil” is literally “was shaken”. Matthew uses the same verb when the earth shakes at the Cross (27:51) and when the guards shake at the tomb (28:4).
vv: Look, your king is coming to you, humble, and mounted on a donkey, and on a colt, the foal of a donkey.

Matthew begins the quotation with words from Isaiah 62:11 and goes on with Zechariah. Only he mentions two animals. He may be following the wording of the Hebrew closely, and wanting to show that every word was fulfilled.
Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest heaven!
Cloaks on the road greeted a new king (2 Kings 9:13). The people are naming Jesus as David’s heir. They are right, though the throne they have in mind may not be the one he is going to.
It is written, ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer’; but you are making it a den of robbers.

He joins Isaiah 56:7 and Jeremiah 7:11. In Jeremiah a den is where robbers go to feel safe between raids: it warns against thinking that worship protects a life of injustice. Jesus loved the Temple, and he acts here as prophets had, out of zeal for his Father’s house (CCC 583–584). This is not an attack on Judaism.
The blind and the lame came to him in the temple, and he cured them.

This verse is found only in Matthew. A saying in 2 Samuel 5:8 had kept the blind and the lame out of “the house”, in connection with David. The Son of David now brings them in and heals them. The Temple is being made what it was meant to be.
Out of the mouths of infants and nursing babies you have prepared praise for yourself
The words are from Psalm 8:2, in the Greek version. The children carry on the cry after the adults have gone, and Jesus defends them. The Church sees here how the small ones know the King.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus entered Jerusalem as the Messiah, acclaimed by children and by God’s poor, and that the Church takes up their Hosanna in the Sanctus (CCC 559); this entry shows the coming of the kingdom that the King-Messiah will bring about by his death and Resurrection (CCC 560). St Andrew of Crete invites us to spread before Christ’s feet not branches but ourselves (in substance). St Augustine says it was no promotion for the Lord of the ages to become King of Israel, but condescension: he came to rule souls (On John 51; in substance).

qa: Did Jesus really ride on two animals?

Mark, Luke and John speak only of the colt. “He sat on them” (v. 7) may refer to the cloaks. Matthew seems to read Zechariah’s words closely and to show them being met in full. St Justin Martyr saw in the two animals a picture of the two peoples called together: Israel, already used to the yoke of the Law, and the Gentiles (Dialogue with Trypho 53; in substance).
Did the same people who shouted Hosanna shout “Crucify him” a few days later?

Preachers often say so, but the Gospel does not. Matthew’s crowd on the road knows Jesus as the prophet “from Nazareth in Galilee” (v. 11), and many think they were pilgrims travelling with him. At the trial he says that “the chief priests and the elders persuaded the crowds” (27:20). The Church teaches that the Jews as a whole cannot be held responsible for his death, and that all sinners were the authors of his Passion (CCC 597–598). The better question is how quickly my own Hosanna can change.
Does Romans 11 mean that God has replaced Israel with the Church?

No. Paul is writing precisely against that idea. God’s gifts and call to Israel are irrevocable (11:29). The Gentile is grafted into Israel’s tree and does not uproot it. The Church lives from that root and awaits the day when all peoples will call on the Lord with one voice (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 839).
rite: Hosanna Sunday is among the most loved days of the Syro-Malabar year. The people gather with tender coconut leaves, the kuruthola. The palms are blessed, the Gospel of the entry is proclaimed, and the procession moves to the church with the cross going before and the Hosanna hymns on every lip. The King we have welcomed with palms then comes to us truly on the altar in the Holy Qurbana. Families take the blessed palm home to the prayer corner, and a cross folded from it is pressed into the Pesaha appam. So the leaf that greeted the King will be on the table of the Lord’s Supper. Today begins Hasha Week, the Week of the Passion. We enter it with our children crying out in front of us, as they did in the Temple, asking only to remain with him when the shouting stops.
study: Zechariah’s king has no warhorse. Where do I still expect God to win by force and not by humility?
“It is not you that support the root.” What have I received from Israel’s Scripture and faith? How should this shape the way I speak of the Jewish people?
When Jesus enters my “temple”, what tables would he overturn? Who are the blind and lame he would bring in?
How can my family walk through Hasha Week together, so that the Hosanna of today is still on our lips on Friday?
